messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jared is a 22-year-old African male and school principal who has been experiencing significant psychological distress following his traumatic childhood experiences of physical abuse by a caregiver. He recently sought help after struggling with increasingly debilitating symptoms that have affected both his personal life and professional responsibilities. Growing up, Jared was subjected to intense physical abuse that left him feeling overwhelmed and helpless. The unpredictability and intensity of these episodes continue to haunt him today. Unpredictable situations, old photos, and waking up from nightmares are potent triggers for Jared’s distress. When he encounters these triggers, they bring back fragmented memories that feel more real than any ordinary recollection. For example, finding an old photo in his parents’ home can immediately transport him back to a moment of intense pain and fear, where the details of the abuse come flooding back but remain disconnected, like pieces of a puzzle that don’t fit together. These vivid flashes of memory are often overwhelming and make it difficult for him to recall events deliberately or piece them together in a coherent narrative. Jared’s fears about his own anger have grown over time. He is certain that he will not be able to control his rage, which has led him to avoid situations where he might lose control. This fear of rage has been exacerbated by the belief that he has permanently changed for the worse and that he remains helplessly vulnerable to bad things happening to him. These negative appraisals feed into each other, creating a cycle of distress. His sense of helplessness is reinforced by his fragmented memories, which make it hard for him to see himself as anything but damaged and fragile. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened during the abuse, the difficulty in accessing these memories only strengthens his belief that something inside him has been permanently altered. These negative appraisals also intensify his reaction to triggers. For instance, waking up from a nightmare leaves him feeling more helpless and angry than ever, leading to further fragmented recollections of past events. This cycle has led Jared to avoid certain situations at work and home, which in turn has strained his relationship with his partner. His avoidance behaviors have had concrete consequences. At work, he finds it increasingly difficult to manage unpredictable situations that could arise during a school day, such as emergencies or conflicts among students. His difficulty in handling these moments has affected his performance and left him feeling even more helpless and frustrated. The distress has become so overwhelming that Jared finally decided to seek help. He is most afraid of losing control and hurting someone, but he also hopes to find ways to manage his memories and negative thoughts so that they do not dictate how he lives his life anymore. Jared’s story highlights the intertwined nature of his triggers, fragmented memories, and negative appraisals, which have collectively created a distressing cycle that has significantly impacted his daily functioning.
